passage: By her third week at the restaurant in Manchester, nobody had said Fatima's name. Head Chef's rule: apprentices are 'Commis', they eat standing after everyone else, and they don't use the staff room. Ada, the sous chef, enforced it with a tired shrug. "Commis, bins. Commis, move." When Fatima sat down once on an upturned crate, Ada said, "Up. Not my rule. I'd get it in the neck." At home Fatima caught herself thinking of her hands as equipment, like the mop. She wrote her own name on a sticky note just to see it. On Friday she rang her college tutor, Mr Hughes, and told him everything. He listened, said, "That's not training, that's being treated like a thing," and emailed the restaurant's owner before she had even hung up.

qa.q: What were apprentices called in the kitchen?
qa.a: Apprentices are 'Commis', so nobody said Fatima's name.

qa.q: What does writing her own name on a sticky note suggest Fatima was feeling?
qa.a: Fatima felt invisible and reduced to equipment, like the mop, and needed to remind herself she was a person.

qa.q: What choice made a difference for Fatima, and how did the tutor respond?
qa.a: Fatima rang Mr Hughes and told him everything; he listened, called it being treated like a thing, and emailed the owner straight away.

qa.q: How does Ada seem to see the rule?
qa.a: Ada treats it as Head Chef's rule, not a personal choice, and fears getting in trouble, even while enforcing it with a tired shrug.

grounding: Shows a junior worker stripped of her name under a head chef's rule enforced by staff who insist it isn't theirs.

passage: Room numbers, not names: that was the 'intro week' rule at the girls' hostel, handed down by Neelam, the senior-most resident. For five nights Gargi was '212'. At dinner seniors called out, "212, stand." "212, sing." "212, explain why you're slow." When Gargi asked one of them, a gentle-looking third-year, why, the girl wouldn't meet her eyes. "Neelam di's orders. If we don't, we get it next." By Friday Gargi had stopped looking up from her plate. She felt like a number on a door, something to be moved about. That night she walked to the warden's office in her slippers and said, "I need to report something." The warden closed the door, listened to all of it, said, "This is ragging, and none of it is on you," and phoned the anti-ragging committee head from the desk while Gargi sat there.

qa.q: What number was Gargi called for five nights?
qa.a: For five nights Gargi was '212'.

qa.q: How was Gargi feeling by Friday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Gargi felt like a number on a door, something to be moved about; she had stopped looking up from her plate.

qa.q: Which step turned things around, and what did the warden do?
qa.a: Gargi went to the warden's office to report it; the warden listened, called it ragging, said none of it was on Gargi, and phoned the anti-ragging committee head right then.

qa.q: How does the third-year seem to see her own part in it?
qa.a: She seems uncomfortable, not meeting Gargi's eyes, and insists she has no choice because refusing would make her the next target.

grounding: Illustrates a fresher reduced to a room number by seniors following the senior-most resident's orders, and an adult acting the same night.

passage:
Farida,
I need to tell someone who isn't at the call centre. Our team lead has a new 'accountability' policy: whoever has the lowest call score each day gets their name on the red board, and the rest of the team has to read out their mistakes at the evening huddle. This week it's been me three times. Yesterday people I eat lunch with read out my 'errors' like a list of charges. Afterwards Rukhsar whispered, 'Sorry yaar, TL's policy, we have no choice.' Everyone says that. Nobody looks at me, only at the board. I've started to feel like a score, not a person.
I'm going to HR tomorrow at nine, and I'm printing the huddle messages tonight. Will you call me after? Just to hear a voice that uses my name.
Deepika

qa.a: Their name goes on the red board, and the rest of the team has to read out their mistakes at the evening huddle.

qa.q: What does 'Just to hear a voice that uses my name' reveal about Deepika?
qa.a: Deepika feels lonely and reduced to a score, and longs to be treated as a person again by someone who cares.

qa.q: What choice has Deepika made, and why is it a strong one?

passage: "You asked why I nearly quit the football academy, Rashmi. Here's the real reason. First month, the captain made a rule: we junior boys carry every senior's kit bag and are called 'Boot Boy' instead of our names. The seniors did it to us every evening, laughing. When I asked one of them, Ravi, why, he said, 'Captain's orders, Jeevan. If I don't, I'm on bags too.' That was the line from everyone: no choice. After three weeks I felt like a peg to hang bags on. I stopped using my own name in my head. Then one night I phoned my coach at home and told him everything. He came to the hostel that same night, said none of it was my fault, stopped the rule on the spot, and reported it to the academy director before morning."

qa.q: What were juniors called instead of their names?
qa.a: They were called 'Boot Boy' instead of their names.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel after three weeks of carrying the seniors' bags?
qa.a: He felt worthless and invisible, like a peg to hang bags on, so much that he stopped using his own name in his head.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it work?
qa.a: Phoning his coach and telling everything brought an adult who came that night, said it was not his fault, stopped the rule and reported it, so the harm ended.

qa.q: How did Ravi see his part in the rule?
qa.a: Ravi saw himself as having no choice, following the captain's orders so he would not end up carrying bags himself.

grounding: A junior footballer targeted by seniors on the captain's orders feels treated as a thing, while those doing it insist they have no choice.

passage: I'm Kavitha, and I shared a room with Shalini in our nursing hostel, so I saw this from close up. Our ward in-charge started a new policy: any trainee who made an error had her name read out at handover and was put on nights for a week. The staff nurses carried it out; they'd say, "Sorry, Shalini, orders," and then read her name like a charge sheet. Shalini, twenty-two, was on nights for three weeks straight. She stopped eating breakfast with us. Once I heard her say, "I'm just the mistake trainee," in a flat voice. I don't know everything she felt, but she looked at people as if she were furniture being moved. One evening I walked her to the principal's office. The principal listened to her for an hour, said the policy was not how anyone should be treated, and called the ward in-charge in that same evening.

qa.q: What happened to a trainee who made an error under the new policy?
qa.a: Her name was read out at handover and she was put on nights for a week.

qa.q: What does Shalini's flat 'I'm just the mistake trainee' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels worthless and defeated, having started to see herself the way the policy treats her, as a label rather than a person.

qa.q: Which choice by Kavitha made a difference, and why?
qa.a: Walking Shalini to the principal's office brought the problem to someone with power, who listened, rejected the policy and called in the ward in-charge that evening.

qa.q: How did the staff nurses see their own part in the policy?
qa.a: They acted as if they had no choice, saying 'Sorry, Shalini, orders' before reading out her name.

grounding: A trainee targeted by a punitive policy carried out on a superior's orders feels treated as a thing, while those enforcing it insist they are only following orders.

passage: In the polytechnic hostel of a small town near Sagar, Ujjwal, eighteen, had been there a week when the seniors knocked. "Sumit bhai's orders," one said. "Freshers clean our rooms. Every day." Ujjwal scrubbed floors while they sat on the bed and laughed. When he paused, one flicked water at him. "Don't look at us. Look at the floor." He felt like a broom, not a boy. At night he lay awake, thinking maybe this was what he was now. On Sunday he saw Sumit and asked, "Why?" Sumit shrugged. "Seniors did it to us. I'm just passing it on." The next morning Ujjwal went to the warden's office and told him everything. The warden wrote it down, called Sumit and the others in that afternoon, and moved Ujjwal to a room near his own quarters that same day.

qa.q: What did the seniors make freshers do every day?

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel while scrubbing floors?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt humiliated and dehumanised, like a broom rather than a boy, starting to see himself as they treated him.

qa.q: Why was going to the warden an important step?
qa.a: It brought an adult with authority into the situation, who acted the same day to stop the ragging and protect Ujjwal.

qa.q: How does Sumit see his own role in the ragging?

grounding: A fresher ragged on a senior's orders feels treated as a thing, while those involved say they are only passing it on, until he reports it.

passage: At the call centre in Buenos Aires, a new rule came down from head office: anyone below target would have their name written in red on the whiteboard, and their chair taken away for the day. Valentina, twenty-two, three weeks into the job, stood for her whole eight-hour shift on Tuesday, headset on, legs aching, her name in red above her. Her supervisor, Noa, avoided her eyes. "It's not my rule," Noa said at the break. "If I don't, I lose my job." Valentina nodded, but inside she felt like a number, not a person. The others walked past her without speaking, as if the red name was contagious. That evening she wrote a calm email to HR, describing the policy and how it felt. HR called her the next morning and suspended the rule while they reviewed it.

qa.q: How long did Valentina stand on Tuesday?
qa.a: She stood for her whole eight-hour shift on Tuesday.

qa.q: How did Valentina feel with her name in red above her?
qa.a: Valentina felt humiliated and dehumanised, like a number rather than a person.

qa.q: What did Valentina do that was wise, and why?
qa.a: She wrote a calm email to HR describing the policy and its effect, which led to the rule being suspended.

qa.q: How does Noa see her part in the policy?

grounding: A junior targeted by a punitive policy carried out on a superior's orders feels treated as a thing, while the supervisor insists she had no choice.

passage:
On his fourth night in the engineering hostel, Karthik was called to the third floor. A row of seniors sat on beds. Ojas, a second-year, handed him a bucket. "Stand on it. Sing. Final years' orders."
Karthik stood on the bucket and sang while they filmed. They called him "Fresher 12," not his name. When his voice cracked, they laughed.
"Why are you doing this?" he asked Ojas.
Ojas shrugged. "Not my choice. They told us to."
Back in his room, Karthik felt like an object on a shelf, not a human being. His hands wouldn't stop shaking. He called the anti-ragging helpline number printed on the hostel wall. The warden came to his room within the hour, stayed with him, and took the seniors' names that night.

qa.q: What did the seniors call Karthik?
qa.a: They called him "Fresher 12."

qa.q: What did Karthik feel back in his room?
qa.a: He felt like an object on a shelf, not a human being, humiliated and so shaken his hands wouldn't stop.

qa.q: Which step helped, and why?
qa.a: Calling the anti-ragging helpline; the warden came within the hour, stayed with him and took the seniors' names that night.

qa.q: How does Ojas see his own part?
qa.a: Ojas insists he had no choice because the final years told them to, which lets him avoid feeling responsible.

grounding: Shows a first-year ragged on seniors' orders who feels treated as an object, while those doing it say they had no choice; he reports it and the warden acts the same night.

Remember how excited I was to start the nursing traineeship? It's different now.
The ward in-charge has a new rule: any trainee who makes a small mistake must clean the sluice room alone, and nobody may speak to her for the day. The staff nurses follow it exactly. When I dropped a tray on Monday, they walked past me like I wasn't there. One said, "Sorry, orders."
I felt like a piece of furniture. Not a person learning.
I don't blame them all. But they chose to follow it.
I've written to the principal of the nursing school today, with dates. She's called me in tomorrow morning. Wish me courage.
Zainab

passage:
Abhinav, you asked about my first week of law school. I'm Salma, and I'll tell you.
Every night, second-years lined us up outside the mess. We had to bow and say, "Good evening, respected senior." If we looked up, we had to start again. They gave us numbers instead of names. I was 34.
One night I asked a senior girl why. She looked tired. "The final years told us to. We have no choice."
But she had a choice. I stood there feeling like a number, not a girl who had come to study law.
On the eighth night I went to the anti-ragging committee office. A professor listened, said it was not my fault, and posted a guard by the mess that same evening.

qa.a: The senior girl feels tired and says she has no choice because the final years told them to.

passage:
Monday, first week of hostel: at 11 pm the seniors called the first-years to the common room. Urmila, a second-year, read from a list: 'Orders from the hostel head. Stand. Face the wall. Answer only yes, ma'am.' Indu stood for two hours. Nobody asked her name. She felt like furniture being arranged.
Wednesday: it happened again. When Indu's legs shook, Urmila whispered, 'Sorry, it's not me, I have no choice,' and still made her stand.
Friday: Indu called her mother at lunch, then walked into the anti-ragging office with her roommate. The warden listened, wrote everything down, and that same evening called in the hostel head and the seniors. The night meetings stopped. The next day Urmila found Indu in the mess and said again, 'I had no choice.' Indu looked at her. 'You did. You just didn't take it.'

qa.q: What did Urmila read from the list?
qa.a: Stand, face the wall and answer only 'yes, ma'am'.

qa.q: How did Indu feel standing for two hours?
qa.a: Indu felt dehumanised and humiliated, like furniture being arranged, with nobody even asking her name.

qa.q: What did the warden's response get right?
qa.a: Listening, recording everything and acting that same evening, calling in the hostel head and the seniors so the meetings stopped.

qa.q: Why does Urmila keep saying she had no choice?
qa.a: Urmila likely feels guilty and wants to push the responsibility onto the hostel head's orders.

grounding: Over a week a first-year ragged on a senior's orders feels treated as a thing, while those doing it claim they had no choice.

passage: Hrithik, before you start at that big office, let me tell you about my first job. I was twenty-one, at a call centre in Gurgaon. Our manager ordered the team leaders to put a paper crown marked SLOWEST on the lowest scorer each evening and make them read their numbers aloud. The first week it was me. The team leader, Bunty, a nice boy who shared his lunch with me, put the crown on my head and read my number like a price tag. I felt like a thing on a shelf, not Simran. Afterwards he said, 'Sorry yaar, orders. I have no choice.' The next day I went to HR with two colleagues and a written complaint. HR stopped the crown that week. Bunty avoided me for a month. I didn't hate him. But I never believed that 'no choice' again.

qa.q: How did Simran feel wearing the crown?

passage: It was exam week, the hostel generator had failed, and at midnight the seniors banged on Sahil's door. 'Sports secretary's orders. All freshers on the ground.' In the dark, Nilesh, a third-year, made them do push-ups on the gravel while shouting their roll numbers, not their names. Sahil, with a chemistry exam in eight hours, asked to go back. Nilesh shone a torch in his face. 'Not my decision, bro. Orders. Keep going.' Sahil felt he had stopped being a person; he was a number doing push-ups. At 1:30 a junior fainted. Sahil ran to the warden's quarters and banged on the door. The warden came out in his vest, stopped everything, called the college doctor and the dean, and sat with the boy until the doctor arrived. By morning the sports secretary and Nilesh were suspended from the hostel pending an inquiry. Sahil sat his exam half-asleep, but he sat it.

qa.q: What were the freshers made to shout?
qa.a: Their roll numbers, not their names.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel doing push-ups on the gravel?
qa.a: Sahil felt dehumanised and frightened, as if he had stopped being a person and become a number.

qa.q: What did the warden do right?
qa.a: He stopped everything at once, called the doctor and the dean, and stayed with the boy who fainted, that same night.

qa.q: How does Nilesh justify what he is doing?
qa.a: Nilesh insists it isn't his decision, claiming he is only following orders.

grounding: During exam week a fresher is ragged on a senior's orders, feels treated as a number, and the warden acts the same night.

passage: In the first week after the Diwali break, the girls' hostel in Pune had a new "rule" from the senior general secretary: first-years were to stand in the corridor at midnight, heads down, and recite their names and marks when asked. Disha stood there on Tuesday, barefoot on cold tiles, while Damini from third year walked the line with a torch. "Name. Marks. Louder." Nobody looked at Disha's face. The torch passed over her as if she were a shelf. "Why are you doing this?" Disha whispered. "Not my rule," Damini said. "GS's orders. I don't have a choice." The next morning Disha called the anti-ragging helpline printed on her admission form and went straight to the warden's office with two other first-years. The warden listened, wrote down every name and, that same afternoon, called a meeting and ended the midnight line.

qa.q: What were first-years made to recite at midnight?
qa.a: Their names and marks.

qa.q: How did Disha feel as the torch passed over her?
qa.a: She felt humiliated and invisible, treated like a thing, a shelf, rather than a person with a face.

qa.q: Which of Disha's steps was wise, and why?
qa.a: Calling the anti-ragging helpline and going to the warden with two other first-years, because it brought in someone with authority, who ended the line that same day.

qa.q: Why might Damini insist she had no choice?
qa.a: Blaming the general secretary's orders lets Damini avoid feeling responsible for hurting juniors, though she chose to walk the line.

grounding: A junior made to stand in a midnight line on a senior's orders feels treated as a thing, while the senior enforcing it claims she had no choice.
